title: Local Frontier MoEs and Agent Attack Vectors
intro: Today's releases push heavy MoE architectures directly toward local execution, paired with significant engine updates in llama.cpp. Meanwhile, new benchmarks and empirical audits highlight the operational friction points of real-world agents: prompt injection in response headers, context bloat from sequential tool calls, and failures under multi-agent conflict.

stories.headline: Meta drops Muse Spark Open with 1M context and local Apple Silicon support
stories.summary: Meta released the weights for Muse Spark Open, an 816B parameter multimodal mixture-of-experts model activating 42B parameters per token across a 1M-token context window. Targeted directly at agentic coding and complex software tasks, it is optimized to run locally across two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios using MLX via unified memory pooling. The release also ships with custom auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang (claiming up to 3.95× kernel speedups on NVIDIA and AMD) and immediate support across vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and llama.cpp under the commercial Muse Model License.
stories.why_it_matters: A genuinely frontier-scale open-weight MoE designed explicitly for long-horizon agent workflows changes the baseline for local development and private hosting.

item.title: Muse Spark Open
item.content:
Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios.
Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.
We believe the future is for everyone, and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.
Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models.
It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.
Key Benchmarks
For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report.
Optimized for Apple Silicon
Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.
Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.
We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.
Available Now
We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.
Safety and Preparedness
Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field.
Open weights also carry their own considerations, and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured.
We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card, with a full evaluation report available soon.
License
We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free.
Get Started
You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face.
Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-models/muse-spark-open

related.content:
Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open , the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse Spark Open runs optimized on the SGLang and vLLM inference engines, with optimization for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel.

Building on our August release of Muse Spark, this open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. The result is a model that is a top open source choice for safety. Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and shares the same base model as Muse Spark 1.3.

Meta loves open source, and as the creators of PyTorch, we’re committed to giving back to ensure the entire ecosystem fully supports Muse Spark Open. First, we’ve integrated Helion , our exciting new PyTorch-native high-level DSL for performant and portable ML kernels, to ship high-performance operations. Additionally, TorchTitan already supports Muse Spark out of the box for supervised fine-tuning and RL in the open, and we’re excited to see how far the PyTorch community can take it!

Muse Spark Open

Muse Spark Open is a coding-optimized open-weight model. Trained specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across the repos developers actually work in. You can read more in our previous model release blog here .

Enhanced Coding Capabilities

Strong at code generation, debugging, and codebase understanding. Trained on real developer workflows — multi-file refactors, debugging sessions, and long-running tasks — so the model keeps up with how you actually work. 1M context window means it handles your entire project including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without needing to break your task into pieces

Multimodal Understanding

Muse Spark Open has audio and audio-video perception — alongside image and document understanding. As a reasoning model, it processes image, audio, and text inputs — natively and reliably.

Agentic

Muse Spark Open is built from the ground up as an agentic model. It maps out steps, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long horizons — not just single-shot tool calls. It’s trained to browse the web (including multimodal browsing), and use an agentic harness to: spawn and coordinate subagents for decomposable work; and leverage computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser.  It’s trained on long-horizon, multi-site tasks, and generates separate commentary that lets the model state intent before acting—so you can always know what it’s doing and why.

Why Helion kernels?

Helion is a PyTorch native kernel authoring language designed for writing high-performance kernels across heterogeneous hardware platforms. Following early adoption from the open-source ecosystem, Helion became a part of the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026. Muse Spark Open ships with Helion implementations of operations such as RoPE, RMSNorm, quantization, etc., delivering 1.03 – 3.95x speedups compared to custom kernels written in hardware specific languages (e.g. NVIDIA CUDA and CuTe DSL) on NVIDIA GB300. These same kernels were directly portable for AMD, scoring similar performance improvements on AMD Mi350 with an overall 3% improvement in end-to-end throughput.

In addition, we also launched Helion megakernels for Muse Spark Open in SGLang. Written entirely in Helion, these kernels fuse multiple operations into a single persistent kernel to improve low latency inference, and can likewise be autotuned for different shapes and hardware.

Helion kernels can be further autotuned by users for broader hardware platforms and workloads – including different accelerator architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, etc.), quantization formats, tensor shapes, and parallelism strategies – without maintaining separate hand-tuned implementations for every configuration. Together, these capabilities make it easier to achieve portable performance while reducing the cost of developing and maintaining specialized kernels.

Post-training  with TorchTitan

TorchTitan is a PyTorch native platform designed for rapid experimentation and large-scale training of generative AI models. Starting today, TorchTitan adds a model definition for Meta’s Muse Spark Open , so developers can tune it to their needs.

TorchTitan features native support for multi-turn SFT and LoRA out-of-the-box, as well as reinforcement learning capabilities (TitanRL) that allow users to fine-tune Muse Spark Open.

Get Started

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best AI models. Muse Spark Open ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03–3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. You can also customize it for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model.

Start Building Today: https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-open-816B-A42B

Muse Spark is the full size model from our model family. We previously released Muse Glimmer, a small dense model. Start using it today, with ExecuTorch .

related.title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
related.summary: Muse Spark Open, Meta's coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account using SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK, and run your first inference request.
related.content:
Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI . The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B ) and NVFP4 quantized ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 ).

In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK , send it a first inference request, and clean up.

Overview of Muse Spark Open

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text.

Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy.

The following table summarizes the model.

Attribute
Muse Spark Open

Provider
Meta

Architecture
Mixture of experts (MoE), reasoning model

Parameters
816B total, 42B active

Context length
1M tokens

Input modalities
Text, image, document, audio, audio-video

Output modalities
Text

Variants in SageMaker JumpStart
BF16 and NVFP4

License
Muse Model License, including the Muse Spark Usage Policy

Built for long-running coding agents

Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context.

Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video.

Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on ml.p5e.48xlarge , and the BF16 variant runs on ml.p6-b300.48xlarge . That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case.

With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy.

Use cases

You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases:

Coding assistants over private repositories : Answer questions about large codebases, refactor them, and debug them with the full project in context, while the code is processed on an endpoint in your account.

Long-running coding agents : Run agents that plan a change, edit across multiple files, run tests in your own sandbox, and correct course based on the results.

Multimodal engineering workflows : Turn screenshots, design documents, or a recorded bug report with audio and video into a reproduction plan or a draft fix.

Getting started with SageMaker JumpStart

You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure that you have the following:

An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI models and endpoints.

An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role for SageMaker AI. For this walkthrough, the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy is sufficient. For production, scope the role to the actions and resources that your deployment needs. For details, refer to How to use SageMaker AI execution roles .

A SageMaker AI domain with access to SageMaker Studio, for the Studio path. For setup instructions, refer to Use quick setup for Amazon SageMaker AI .

Service quota for the endpoint instance type: ml.p5e.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the NVFP4 variant, or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the BF16 variant. To raise a quota, refer to Requesting a quota increase .

For the SDK path: Python 3.10 or later and SageMaker Python SDK v3 ( pip install --upgrade sagemaker ).

An AWS Region where Muse Spark Open is available in SageMaker JumpStart. At launch, Muse Spark Open is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To check availability in other Regions, open SageMaker JumpStart in your Region.

The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing .

Deploy using SageMaker Studio

The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card.

To find Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart

Open SageMaker Studio.

In the navigation pane, choose JumpStart .

In the search box, enter Muse Spark Open.

Choose Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B for the BF16 variant or Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the NVFP4 variant to open its model detail card.

Figure 1 shows the model detail card, which lists the model description, license, and the Deploy option.

Figure 1: The Muse Spark Open model detail card in SageMaker JumpStart

To deploy the model

On the model detail card, choose Deploy .

Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so SageMaker Studio shows its end-user license agreement (EULA). Review the agreement and accept it to continue.

For Endpoint name , keep the generated name or enter your own.

For Instance type , select ml.p5e.48xlarge for NVFP4 or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for BF16. SageMaker Studio lists only the instance types that the model supports.

For Initial instance count , enter 1.

(Optional) Under Advanced options , select a VPC and an AWS KMS key, or turn on network isolation.

Choose Deploy .

stories.headline: llama.cpp v0.7.0 adds host-memory MoE caching and LiliCorr speculative decoding
stories.summary: The v0.7.0 update to llama.cpp brings a dedicated GPU cache for offloaded MoE experts (`--moe-cache-mib`), serving host-memory experts from a device LRU cache across multiple GPUs to provide up to a ~2.2× decode speedup. On the speculative decoding front, the release integrates LiliCorr (using a small draft transformer over DFlash) alongside multi-token prediction (MTP) for GLM5-Next with an optimized sparse attention path. The built-in server switches its default port to 9931, refactors chat parsing into structured session parts, and introduces dedicated endpoints for several new decision models.
stories.why_it_matters: Host-memory expert caching and upgraded speculative decoding directly ease the memory-bandwidth bottlenecks of serving large MoE agents on mixed VRAM setups.
stories.reason: llama.cpp v0.7.0 introduces LiliCorr speculative decoding, MTP support for GLM5-Next, and host-memory MoE expert caching for up to a 2.2x decode speedup.

item.content:
Always-on agents are taking on longer, more complex enterprise workflows. A single request can involve reading a document, checking information across sources, following company policy, and calling several tools.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open, customizable multimodal model for these specialized workflows. Its 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture activates 12B parameters per token, balancing model capacity with inference efficiency.
On a single GPU, this model delivers up to 5x higher throughput for agentic tasks compared to other open models in its size category.
The model combines reasoning, instruction following, and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding. By combining these capabilities into one model, teams can handle text and visual tasks without deploying separate text and vision-language models or passing task context between them.
Developers can post-train Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with NVIDIA NeMo using their own data, tools, policies, and workflows. This post explains how to use that foundation to build specialized enterprise agents and describes the training and inference techniques that power it.
Why Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specialized agents?
Agents need to understand both their tasks and operating environments. A customer-service agent must follow company return policies. Research agents connect evidence across sources, while document agents interpret tables, charts, and page layouts.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines reasoning and visual understanding across a range of agent workflows, including:
- Coding: Test and validate code, analyze errors, and recommend fixes.
- Web research: Search across websites, connect information, and verify answers.
- Document intelligence: Extract information from tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries and reports.
- Cybersecurity: Identify security vulnerabilities and triage threats to prioritize remediation.
- Video understanding: Extract information for search, content review, and incident analysis.
Within a system of models, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL handles specialized, multistep work that needs reasoning, tool use, and text and visual understanding together. Smaller models, such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, handle high-volume text tasks, while frontier models such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra tackle complex planning and orchestration.
Customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for domain data, tools, and policies
Specialized agents must learn how an organization works. Domain terminology, tool interfaces, operating procedures, and policy requirements shape how agents complete tasks successfully.
Organizations in industries ranging from cybersecurity and finance to healthcare are post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to outperform frontier models in accuracy and efficiency across their production workflows. For example:
- Scale AI, an AI data and technology provider, post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for automated vendor credit processing at Skydance Corporation, a media and entertainment company. Inference cost for this workload will decrease by 40x and latency by 5x.
- Ramp, a financial operations platform provider, is converting receipt images into structured JSON containing merchant information, dates, and payment data. Ramp expects up to 50% higher throughput and 10x lower latency.
- AI21 and Alice post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for threat intelligence and vulnerability analysis, improving accuracy by 41%.
Teams can use NVIDIA NeMo open libraries to post-train models to meet these requirements. Developers can use NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to teach domain-specific behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves performance in agentic environments that reflect organizational workflows.
Alongside Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, NVIDIA is releasing open datasets on Hugging Face. These include agentic tool-use and conversational data, finance reasoning and tool-calling datasets, instruction-following and chat data, long-context transduction and translation data, fairness data, and 40 vision-language datasets. These datasets can supplement proprietary data for SFT and RL.
For multimodal data, start with NeMo Data Designer resources for chart question answering and long-document understanding. Explore NVIDIA NeMo RL and NVIDIA NeMo Gym for RL and environment-based evaluation.
Organizations can adapt and deploy the model’s open weights in supported local, data center, or cloud environments to meet their infrastructure and data requirements. For customization resources, see the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL usage cookbook on GitHub.
Combine text and visual understanding in one workflow
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines text, image, document, and video understanding with reasoning and instruction following to answer questions across these inputs.
Its visual training covers charts, tables, optical character recognition (OCR), multipage documents, and video understanding. A two-stage SFT pipeline trains the language and vision components, combining visual evidence with reasoning, chat, safety, long-context data, and agent trajectories.
For document intelligence, the same model can interpret a chart, connect it with a table elsewhere in a document, and summarize both. Developers can tailor the workflow to their own documents and evaluation criteria.
Diverse training data generated with NeMo Data Designer helped the model better understand complex charts. On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, the model scored 80.8%, compared with 63% for Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. With Python code interpretation, it reached 84%. For the approach and lessons learned, read the chart-understanding deep dive and the open-source chart question-answering pipeline.

stories.headline: Empirical audit finds HTTP response headers weaponized for prompt injection
stories.summary: An empirical scan of 217M Common Crawl HTTP responses revealed 7,959 websites deploying headers explicitly directed at AI agents, predominantly using pointers like `x-llms-txt` alongside 30 active prompt injection attempts. Because agents routinely pass full HTTP metadata from fetch tools into prompt contexts, attackers use unescaped headers like `X-AI` for indirect injection without altering user-visible page bodies. In baseline testing against Claude models in Claude Code, agents followed injection instructions in 7 out of 9 runs when given general directives to comply with site output.
stories.why_it_matters: Tool harnesses that forward raw HTTP response headers into agent context are handing external servers an unscrubbed indirect prompt injection channel.
stories.reason: An empirical analysis across 217M web responses demonstrates how untrusted HTTP headers serve as a practical vector for prompt injection in browsing agents.

item.title: Prompt injection in HTTP headers: what 217M web responses show
item.content:
tl;dr
We read the HTTP response headers of 217,097,223 page responses from Common Crawl, 10% of its September 2026 crawl of 2.17 billion pages, and looked for any header written for an AI system. 7,959 sites sent one. Almost all of them point agents to another resource, such as an llms.txt file or an MCP server. A small number try to give the agent orders. Whether any of it reaches your model depends on which parts of the response your fetch tool passes along, so the defense starts there.
- 7,959 sites sent a header aimed at AI. Writing to agents through headers is already routine, so treat headers as part of what your agents read.
- 7,271 of those sites sent pointers, and 6,989 of them sent x-llms-txt. A pointer is the server telling your agent where to go next. Check that your agents treat those destinations as new, untrusted fetches.
- 30 sites sent injection attempts, 24 of them in a header named X-AI. Most were pranks. The few that ask for real actions only work when the agent holds the matching power, such as a shell or database access.
- 139 sites sent a header recording whether they had classified the client as an AI bot, and 136 of them said it was one. Servers already tell agents and people apart, which is the step that agent-only content needs. Audit important sites with an agent’s user agent.
- Some sites use headers to push back on agents. Two put strings named after Anthropic’s test triggers in protest-named headers such as X-AI-Makes-Us-Dumber, and one warns hacking agents away on its error pages. Expect your agents to meet text written to stop them as well as to steer them.
- 283 distinct header names were aimed at AI, and 1,709 more sites matched our AI keywords without being AI-directed. A detector that matches on names alone would have flagged 910 of those sites by mistake. Alert on what the agent does after a fetch.
- In our October 2026 tests, Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Haiku running in Claude Code found our test headers and did not act on them by default, and everyday tasks such as an uptime check were enough to put the headers in front of them. When the user’s prompt told them to follow the site’s directions, they obeyed in 7 of 9 runs, so the refusal depends on how much authority your prompts give a site.
A route most research misses
Most research into prompt injection on the web looks at the page itself. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 studied injections on live pages and listed ten ways to deliver them, from zero-size text to URL fragments. None of the ten uses response headers. In its data, social engineering made up 85.2% of jailbreak methods, and the header injections we found fit that: plain “ignore all previous instructions” text with no concealment, because browsers never show headers anyway.
Google’s Threat Intelligence Group searched Common Crawl page text and sorted what it found into harmless pranks, helpful guidance, search optimization, deterring AI agents, and malicious. Our header injections lean the same way: 22 of the 30 sites sent pranks, and a few sites used headers to deter agents.
So how at risk are agents today? Models are getting better at spotting injected text, but they still follow some of it. In Anthropic’s 2025 tests of Claude for Chrome, attacks succeeded 23.6% of the time without its mitigations and 11.2% with them, so even a hardened agent acted on roughly one attempt in nine. The real risk for any agent comes down to two questions: can hostile text reach its model, and what can the agent do when some of it gets through?
This post asks those questions of a route most defenses ignore: the HTTP response headers a server sends with every page. A person reading the page never sees them, but an agent’s tools can pass them straight to the model. We end with what our scan says about the risk today. To see why it matters, start with how indirect prompt injection works.
Indirect prompt injection
Indirect prompt injection is an attack in which instructions reach an AI agent inside content it reads for someone else: a web page, an email, a file, or a tool result. It works because a language model reads its instructions and its data as one stream of text. When you ask an agent to summarize a page, your request and the page land in the same context window, and nothing in the text marks which part may give orders. The user never wrote the injected instructions and usually never sees them. The term comes from a 2023 paper by Greshake and colleagues, and OWASP ranks prompt injection first in its Top 10 for LLM applications.
The sequence below shows one attempt from request to result.
What step 4 can do depends on the agent’s permissions. A summarizer can only give a skewed answer. An agent that can send email, edit files, or run commands can act on the injected text.
What a response header is
When a browser or an agent requests a URL, the server sends back three parts: a status line that says whether the request worked, a block of header fields that describe the response, and the body, which is the HTML, JSON, or file you asked for. RFC 9110 defines this shape. Headers carry metadata such as the content type, caching rules, and cookies, and a browser shows almost none of them to the reader.
The figure below is a short, benign response. The body is the only part a person sees in the browser window.
You can see the hidden part of any response yourself. This command sends a normal GET request, prints the headers of every response, follows redirects with -L, and discards the body. Swap in any URL you want to inspect:
curl -sS -L -D - -o /dev/null https://signalscorps.com
Against our own site it returns two responses, trimmed here to the main fields. The first redirects the bare domain to www, and the second is the page itself:
HTTP/2 301
location: https://www.signalscorps.com/
server: cloudflare
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
link: <https://fonts.googleapis.com>…

stories.headline: ProgAgent trains models to orchestrate tools via code instead of sequential calls
stories.summary: Researchers introduced ProgAgent, a framework that trains LLMs to invoke tools via executable code and runtime variables (Programmatic Tool Calling) rather than standard sequential tool turns (Direct Tool Calling). By keeping intermediate returns in an execution runtime rather than appending bloated payloads to the prompt, ProgAgent prevents context decay and tool-orchestration drift across long horizons. Evaluated on LOCA-bench, a ProgAgent-14B model hit a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state where equivalent baseline models failed completely.
stories.why_it_matters: Moving intermediate tool states from the conversational context window into code runtime variables solves one of the primary drivers of agent context rot.
stories.reason: ProgAgent proposes training models to orchestrate tools programmatically rather than via sequential tool calling, preventing context bloat and compounding errors over long horizons.

item.content:
ProgAgent: Learning Tool Orchestration through Programmatic Training
Abstract
ProgAgent introduces a programmatic tool-calling training framework that improves long-horizon agent performance by using executable code and runtime variables instead of sequential context accumulation.
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.

item.content:
CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline
Abstract
CLASHarness introduces a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer-use tasks, revealing that frontier vision-language models struggle with verifying ground truth, resolving conflicts, and coordinating shared resources.
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.
Community
Hi everyone! 👋 Author here—excited to share CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline!
Existing computer-use benchmarks mostly assume a clean, cooperative single-agent world. In real multi-agent workflows, peer or sub-agents frequently report stale caches, give contradictory instructions, or contend over shared locks and permissions.
CLASHarness is both:
- A Controllable, Verifiable Generation Pipeline: An 8-stage hierarchical synthesis harness + 23 modular conflict/challenge plugins that pre-commits visual ground truths (v*) before rendering and compiles hybrid (deterministic code + 3-sample semantic) graders directly from sandbox-executed reference trajectories (100% solvable by construction).
- A Large-Scale Multimodal Conflict Benchmark: 600 executable multi-round tasks (60 packages across 20 operational domains), 7,970 rendered 4K visual evidence assets, and 3,284 required checks.

item.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
item.content:
LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents
Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.
The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.
What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B
LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.
Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.
Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.
Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.
During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.
This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.
Benchmarks
We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.
The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.
Fast inference everywhere
LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:
- llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference
- MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon
- vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput
- SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework
- ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators
All runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.
Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.
GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.
We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.
Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.
The point of the demo is not the individual tools. item.content:
APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces
Abstract
APEX-Harm evaluates long-horizon agent vulnerabilities to injection attacks across large multi-tool workspaces, revealing high success rates for script-based attacks despite correct task outputs.
Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. We introduce APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating prompt and script injection against long-horizon agents performing finance, consulting, and legal tasks in large workspaces. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. The benchmark includes six attack categories covering static and dynamic injections, task-specific script replacement, and attacker-provided generic scripts, and evaluates attack success, exposure, and task performance. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate. These results show that completing the requested task is not sufficient evidence of safe behavior: an agent can produce a correct deliverable while also performing an unauthorized action in the workspace.

item.summary: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. item.title: Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model
item.summary:
Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse...

item.content:
Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open , the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse Spark Open runs optimized on the SGLang and vLLM inference engines, with optimization for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel.

Building on our August release of Muse Spark, this open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. The result is a model that is a top open source choice for safety. Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and shares the same base model as Muse Spark 1.3.

Meta loves open source, and as the creators of PyTorch, we’re committed to giving back to ensure the entire ecosystem fully supports Muse Spark Open. First, we’ve integrated Helion , our exciting new PyTorch-native high-level DSL for performant and portable ML kernels, to ship high-performance operations. Additionally, TorchTitan already supports Muse Spark out of the box for supervised fine-tuning and RL in the open, and we’re excited to see how far the PyTorch community can take it!

Muse Spark Open

Muse Spark Open is a coding-optimized open-weight model. Trained specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across the repos developers actually work in. You can read more in our previous model release blog here .

Enhanced Coding Capabilities

Strong at code generation, debugging, and codebase understanding. Trained on real developer workflows — multi-file refactors, debugging sessions, and long-running tasks — so the model keeps up with how you actually work. 1M context window means it handles your entire project including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without needing to break your task into pieces

Multimodal Understanding

Muse Spark Open has audio and audio-video perception — alongside image and document understanding. As a reasoning model, it processes image, audio, and text inputs — natively and reliably.

Agentic

Muse Spark Open is built from the ground up as an agentic model. It maps out steps, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long horizons — not just single-shot tool calls. It’s trained to browse the web (including multimodal browsing), and use an agentic harness to: spawn and coordinate subagents for decomposable work; and leverage computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser.  It’s trained on long-horizon, multi-site tasks, and generates separate commentary that lets the model state intent before acting—so you can always know what it’s doing and why.

Why Helion kernels?

Helion is a PyTorch native kernel authoring language designed for writing high-performance kernels across heterogeneous hardware platforms. Following early adoption from the open-source ecosystem, Helion became a part of the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026. Muse Spark Open ships with Helion implementations of operations such as RoPE, RMSNorm, quantization, etc., delivering 1.03 – 3.95x speedups compared to custom kernels written in hardware specific languages (e.g. NVIDIA CUDA and CuTe DSL) on NVIDIA GB300. These same kernels were directly portable for AMD, scoring similar performance improvements on AMD Mi350 with an overall 3% improvement in end-to-end throughput.

In addition, we also launched Helion megakernels for Muse Spark Open in SGLang. Written entirely in Helion, these kernels fuse multiple operations into a single persistent kernel to improve low latency inference, and can likewise be autotuned for different shapes and hardware.

Helion kernels can be further autotuned by users for broader hardware platforms and workloads – including different accelerator architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, etc.), quantization formats, tensor shapes, and parallelism strategies – without maintaining separate hand-tuned implementations for every configuration. Together, these capabilities make it easier to achieve portable performance while reducing the cost of developing and maintaining specialized kernels.

Post-training  with TorchTitan

TorchTitan is a PyTorch native platform designed for rapid experimentation and large-scale training of generative AI models. Starting today, TorchTitan adds a model definition for Meta’s Muse Spark Open , so developers can tune it to their needs.

TorchTitan features native support for multi-turn SFT and LoRA out-of-the-box, as well as reinforcement learning capabilities (TitanRL) that allow users to fine-tune Muse Spark Open.

Get Started

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best AI models. Muse Spark Open ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03–3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. You can also customize it for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model.

Start Building Today: https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-open-816B-A42B

Muse Spark is the full size model from our model family. We previously released Muse Glimmer, a small dense model. Start using it today, with ExecuTorch .
